conversation.content: Let's design a social media feed — like Twitter or Instagram. Users post content, follow other users, and see a feed of posts from people they follow. What would you like to clarify?
How many users? And are posts just text or also images and videos?

500 million daily active users. Posts are text with optional images. Let's focus on the feed generation — when a user opens the app, how do they see the latest posts from people they follow? What other requirements matter?
The feed should load fast — maybe under a second? And it should be sorted by time, most recent first. I guess we also need to handle people with lots of followers, like celebrities.
Good — the celebrity problem is one of the hardest parts. Feed should load in under 200ms. Let's start designing. How would you generate a user's feed?

The straightforward approach: when a user opens the app, we look up who they follow, then fetch the most recent posts from all those people, merge them together sorted by time, and return the top 20 or so. It's like a SQL join — SELECT * FROM posts WHERE author_id IN (list of followed users) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20.

That would work logically. But consider: a user follows 500 people, and you're doing this for 500 million users. That query — 'fetch recent posts from 500 different authors and merge' — at 200ms, for millions of concurrent requests. What's the problem?
It would be really slow. You're doing 500 lookups per feed request. At millions of requests per second, that's billions of post lookups. The database would be crushed.

Right. So instead of building the feed when the user asks for it (fan-out-on-read), what if we pre-built the feed ahead of time? When someone posts, we could push that post to all their followers' feeds. This is called fan-out-on-write. What do you think?

Oh, that makes sense. So when User A posts something, we look up all of A's followers and add the post to each follower's precomputed feed. Then when a follower opens the app, their feed is already ready — just read it. That's much faster for reads.
Good. But what happens when a celebrity with 50 million followers posts? You'd need to write to 50 million feeds instantly. That's the celebrity problem you mentioned earlier.

Oh... that's a lot of writes. For one post. It would take forever and overwhelm the system. So maybe we don't do fan-out-on-write for celebrities? Like, for regular users we pre-push to followers' feeds. But for celebrities, we fetch their latest posts at read time and merge them in. A hybrid approach.
That's exactly the hybrid approach that Twitter used. Where would you store these precomputed feeds?

In Redis, probably. Each user has a list in Redis that contains the post IDs of their feed, sorted by time. When a new post is pushed, we prepend it to the list and trim to keep, say, the latest 1000 posts. Redis is fast enough for this — reads and writes to a list are O(1).
Redis list per user with post IDs — that's a common pattern. How much memory would that require? 500 million users, each with a feed.

Hmm, if each feed has 1000 post IDs, and each ID is 8 bytes (a 64-bit integer)... that's 8KB per user. Times 500 million users... that's 4 terabytes. That's a lot for Redis. Maybe we don't store feeds for all users — only active users? Or use a smaller feed size, like 200 posts.

Good attempt at the math. 4TB is actually manageable with a Redis cluster — split across 40 machines with 128GB each. But only caching active users is a smart optimization. What about the posts themselves — where are they stored?

A regular database like PostgreSQL. A posts table with post_id, author_id, content, image_url, created_at, like_count, retweet_count. When the client loads the feed, it gets the list of post IDs from Redis, then fetches the full post details from the database. We could also cache popular posts in Redis to avoid database hits.
What if the user scrolls down and wants older posts — pagination. How does that work with the Redis feed list?

Redis lists support range queries — LRANGE key start end. For the first page, get items 0-19. For the next page, 20-39. The client would pass a cursor or page number. Actually, offset-based pagination can be inconsistent if new posts are added between page loads — the whole list shifts. A better approach might be cursor-based: 'give me 20 posts older than post ID X.' That's stable across inserts.
Good catch on cursor-based pagination. We're running out of time — anything else?

A few things: we'd need a social graph service to manage follow/unfollow relationships. A notification system to alert users of interactions — likes, retweets, follows. And content moderation to filter out spam and harmful content before it appears in feeds.
Good job. You understood the core trade-off between fan-out-on-read and fan-out-on-write, which is the most important concept. Keep practicing capacity estimation. Thanks!

strengths: Understood the hybrid fan-out approach when guided to it — correctly identified the celebrity exception
Good practical solution with Redis feed lists and cursor-based pagination
Memory estimation attempt was reasonable even if rough
weaknesses: Required heavy hinting — didn't arrive at fan-out-on-write independently
No failure handling discussed — what if Redis crashes? What about feed consistency?
No discussion of feed ranking (algorithmic vs chronological) — only mentioned time-sorted
Requirements gathering was minimal — didn't ask about real-time updates, like/retweet propagation, or search
No API design — didn't define the feed API endpoints or response format
